w2-q1: Correct — the topic in a published message gives the broker the routing information to deliver it to matching subscribers.
Incorrect — the client identifier names the client; it is not used to route messages.
Incorrect — payload length describes message size, not where the message should be delivered.
Incorrect — a session timer relates to connection or session handling, not message routing.
w2-q2: Correct — the plus sign is a single-level wildcard matching an arbitrary value at exactly one hierarchy level.
Correct — the hash sign is a multilevel wildcard that subscribes to all underlying hierarchy levels.
Incorrect — house/# matches all topics whose hierarchy begins with house, not only the exact topic house.
Correct — the single-level wildcard in house/+/temperature matches house/kitchen/temperature.
w2-q3: Correct — setup is the first of the four main SMQTT stages.
Correct — publish is one of the four SMQTT stages.
Correct — decryption is the final of the four SMQTT stages.
Incorrect — route discovery is a routing concept and is not an SMQTT stage; the stages are setup, encryption, publish and decryption.
w2-q4: Incorrect — CoAP is designed to avoid the overhead of TCP and runs over UDP instead.
Correct — CoAP runs over UDP, whose lightweight nature suits resource-constrained IoT devices.
Incorrect — CoAP is not defined over SCTP; it uses UDP.
Incorrect — FTP is an application-layer file transfer protocol, not a transport protocol.
w2-q5: Correct — a piggyback response travels inside the acknowledgment, while in separate mode the acknowledgment comes first and the response follows later.
Incorrect — the statement correctly describes both CoAP response modes, so it is true.
w2-q6: Correct — GET maps to retrieving data, as presented in the lecture.
Correct — PUT maps to creating data, as presented in the lecture.
Correct — as presented in the lecture, PUSH maps to updating data.
Correct — DELETE maps to deleting data.
w2-q7: Incorrect — the Transfer frame carries messages rather than controlling flow rate.
Incorrect — the Detach frame terminates a link.
Incorrect — the Disposition frame communicates a change in transfer state.
Correct — the Flow frame controls the rate of message flow between AMQP peers.
w2-q8: Correct — an exchange receives messages and routes them to queues.
Correct — a queue stores messages for consumers or business processes.
Correct — a binding defines the distribution rules between an exchange and queues.
Incorrect — routing is done by the exchange using bindings, not by a consumer before messages reach the exchange.
w2-q9: Correct — IEEE 802.15.4c is associated with China.
Correct — IEEE 802.15.4e is associated with industrial applications.
Correct — IEEE 802.15.4f is associated with active RFID.
Correct — IEEE 802.15.4g is associated with smart utility networks.
w2-q10: Incorrect — slotted CSMA/CA is used in beacon-enabled networks with a superframe structure.
Correct — non-beacon-enabled IEEE 802.15.4 networks transmit data frames using unslotted CSMA/CA.
Incorrect — token passing is not the access method used by IEEE 802.15.4.
Incorrect — non-beacon-enabled networks use unslotted CSMA/CA, not pure TDMA.
w2-q11: Correct — IEEE 802.15.4 specifies the physical and MAC layers, and ZigBee builds on them with higher-layer functions such as routing and mesh networking.
Incorrect — the roles are reversed; IEEE 802.15.4 covers the lower layers and ZigBee adds the higher ones.
Incorrect — neither operates only at the application layer; 802.15.4 covers the physical and MAC layers.
Incorrect — they are distinct; ZigBee extends IEEE 802.15.4 with higher-layer functionality.
w2-q12: Correct — a ZigBee end device has enough functionality to communicate with its parent node.
Correct — an end device cannot relay data for other devices.
Correct — an end device is a reduced-functionality device.
Incorrect — forming the network root and acting as trust center is the role of the coordinator, not an end device.
w2-q13: Incorrect — it is reversed; the 64-bit extended address is globally unique, while the 16-bit address is PAN-specific.
Correct — the 16-bit short address is PAN-specific and assigned by the PAN coordinator, while the 64-bit extended address is globally unique.
Incorrect — the 16-bit short address is PAN-specific and assigned by the PAN coordinator, not globally unique.
Incorrect — these address types are used for general addressing, not only multicast.
w2-q14: Incorrect — in LOADng, intermediate routers may not respond to an RREQ even with an active route, so the statement is false.
Correct — only the destination may respond to an RREQ in LOADng; intermediate routers are prohibited from replying.
w2-q15: Incorrect — passive RFID tags have no internal battery; active tags have their own power supply.
Correct — a passive tag is powered inductively by an RFID reader before it can transmit information.
Incorrect — a wired AIDC connection is not how passive tags are powered; the reader powers them inductively.
Incorrect — a passive tag does need power, which it gets inductively from the reader.
